demo_steps.title: Source-like overview
demo_steps.narration: The full composition is visible at once: separate s, px, py, and pz orbitals on the left, four equivalent sp3 hybrids on the right, and their combined tetrahedral arrangement below.

demo_steps.title: Four distinct starting orbitals
demo_steps.narration: Before hybridization, the orbitals have different shapes and orientations: one spherical s orbital and three perpendicular p orbitals along x, y, and z.

demo_steps.title: Four equivalent sp3 hybrids
demo_steps.narration: Hybridization mixes one s orbital with three p orbitals to form four equivalent sp3 orbitals. Each individual hybrid has a large bonding lobe and a small back-lobe.

demo_steps.title: Tetrahedral arrangement
demo_steps.narration: When the four equivalent hybrids are drawn from the same central atom, their large lobes point toward the corners of a tetrahedron. Orbit this view to see the three-dimensional separation.

demo_steps.title: Optional bond-angle measurement
demo_steps.narration: Turning on the angle marker identifies the characteristic tetrahedral separation of about 109.5°, while keeping it off preserves the cleaner source-figure appearance.

plan.geometry_notes: Use a chemistry-textbook oblique projection, not a perspective view: +X maps horizontally to screen-right, +Z maps vertically upward, and +Y maps diagonally up-right/receding at roughly 30–40 degrees. Keep this same axis convention for every small panel. Overview layout should match the source composition: atomic-orbital block on the upper left, individual sp3-hybrid block on the upper right, final tetrahedral diagram centered below the hybrid block and slightly toward the middle. In overview screen-plane coordinates, place the atomic block centers at approximately s=(-5.4, 2.5), px=(-3.4, 2.5), py=(-5.4, 0.8), pz=(-3.4, 0.8). Place the individual sp3 centers at approximately h1=(1.0, 2.5), h2=(3.0, 2.5), h3=(1.0, 0.8), h4=(3.0, 0.8). Place the final tetrahedral origin at approximately (0.3, -2.1), scaled larger than the small panels. Leave clear spacing between the two-by-two panels so labels and axes do not overlap. Local axis triads in small panels span about 0.9 world units from origin to arrowhead; final tetrahedral axes or guide lines, if shown, may span about 1.4 world units. The s orbital is a translucent sphere radius about 0.38–0.42, colored blue #4f83c4 with glossy highlights. Each p orbital uses two tapered lobes of length about 0.85–0.95 and maximum radius about 0.30–0.34, meeting at the origin. Phase coloring should match the source convention explicitly: px has the red/pink lobe #ef6b73 on +x/right and the blue lobe #4f83c4 on -x/left; py has the red/pink lobe on +y, the diagonal up-right/receding side, and the blue lobe on -y, the lower-left/front side; pz has the red/pink lobe on +z/up and the blue lobe on -z/down. The individual sp3 hybrids use orange/yellow #f6a21a with bright highlight #ffd36b and opacity about 0.85; each has one large teardrop lobe length about 1.0 and radius about 0.34–0.38 plus a small opposite back-lobe length about 0.25–0.30 and radius about 0.10–0.14. In the final tetrahedral arrangement, scale the large lobes to about 1.15–1.25 length and the small back-lobes to about 0.25 length. Use four normalized tetrahedral directions with equal pairwise angles, then rotate them to match the source projection: one large lobe projects nearly vertical upward, one projects down-right/rightward, one projects down-left/back, and one projects downward/front so the final diagram reads as a symmetric tetrahedral cluster. Mathematically the four hybrids may be represented by sign combinations h1=(s+px+py+pz)/2, h2=(s+px-py-pz)/2, h3=(s-px+py-pz)/2, and h4=(s-px-py+pz)/2; all four final hybrid lobes must be equal in size when shown together. Dominant colors: black axes and labels #000000, grey arrows and explanatory text #8a8a8a, blue orbital phase #4f83c4, red/pink orbital phase #ef6b73, orange/yellow hybrid lobes #f6a21a/#ffd36b. Do not show the 109.5° annotation by default; it should only appear when showAngle is true.
plan.notes: Render the overall diagram as a fixed source-like oblique composition in Overview mode. Focused modes may enlarge the selected block and dim or hide the other blocks, but must preserve the same axis orientation: x right, z up, y diagonal up-right. Orbit control should primarily affect the focused Tetrahedral arrangement; in Overview mode keep the layout fixed to avoid destroying the textbook composition. Use smooth parametric or metaball-like orbital meshes rather than simple ellipsoids: p orbitals should taper into the nucleus, and sp3 hybrids should have a clearly dominant large lobe plus a much smaller back-lobe. Use CSS2D or signed-distance text for italic x, y, z and orbital labels. Keep guide lines and optional angle annotation subtle and hidden unless requested so the rendered figure remains visually faithful to the original.

authoredPrompt: This figure illustrates the sp3 hybridization process as a stepwise transformation, moving from four distinct atomic orbitals on the left to four equivalent hybrid orbitals on the right and finally to the tetrahedral arrangement they collectively produce at the bottom. The upper-left section shows the four pre-hybridization atomic orbitals drawn individually on Cartesian axes: a spherical s orbital (blue), a px orbital (two-lobed, red and blue, oriented along the x-axis), a py orbital (two-lobed, oriented along the y-axis), and a pz orbital (two-lobed, oriented along the z-axis). A rightward arrow labeled "Hybridization" leads to four equivalent sp3 hybrid orbitals, each rendered as a prominent orange lobe with a small back-lobe, shown individually pointing in different directions; a downward arrow then labeled "Gives a tetrahedral arrangement" leads to a final diagram in which all four sp3 orbitals appear simultaneously, with their large lobes directed symmetrically toward the four corners of a tetrahedron at 109.5° with respect to each other. This figure demonstrates how the mathematical mixing of one s and three p orbitals destroys the original orbital distinctions and produces four energetically and geometrically equivalent sp3 hybrids that underpin the tetrahedral bond angles observed in molecules such as CH4, NH3, and H2O.
authoredInteractions: - Toggle individual atomic orbital contributions (s, px, py, pz) on and off: isolate each orbital and see its role in forming the tetrahedral hybrid
authoredContext:
The valence orbitals of an atom surrounded by a tetrahedral arrangement of bonding pairs and lone pairs consist of a set of four sp 3 hybrid orbitals . The hybrids result from the mixing of one s orbital and all three p orbitals that produces four identical sp 3 hybrid orbitals ( ). Each of these hybrid orbitals points toward a different corner of a tetrahedron.

The hybridization of an s orbital (blue) and three p orbitals (red) produces four equivalent sp 3 hybridized orbitals (yellow) oriented at 109.5° with respect to each other.

A series of three diagrams connected by a right-facing arrow that is labeled, “Hybridization,” and a downward-facing arrow labeled, “Gives a tetrahedral arrangement,” are shown. The first diagram shows a blue spherical orbital and three red, peanut-shaped orbitals, each placed on an x, y, z axis system. The three red orbitals are located on the x , y and z axes, respectively. The second diagram shows the same four orbitals, but they are now purple and have one enlarged lobe and one smaller lobe. Each lies in a different axis in the drawing. The third diagram shows the same four orbitals, but their smaller lobes now overlap to form a tetrahedral structure.

A molecule of methane, CH 4 , consists of a carbon atom surrounded by four hydrogen atoms at the corners of a tetrahedron. The carbon atom in methane exhibits sp 3 hybridization. We illustrate the orbitals and electron distribution in an isolated carbon atom and in the bonded atom in CH 4 in . The four valence electrons of the carbon atom are distributed equally in the hybrid orbitals, and each carbon electron pairs with a hydrogen electron when the C–H bonds form.

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: The learner follows the transformation from one s and three p orbitals, to four equivalent sp3 hybrids, to the tetrahedral geometry produced by placing all four hybrids around one atom

interactions.label: s contribution
interactions.teaches: The spherical s contribution is the equal component present in every sp3 hybrid, making the four hybrids equivalent rather than preserving separate p-orbital identities

interactions.label: px contribution
interactions.teaches: The px contribution separates hybrids with positive and negative x character, helping aim the final lobes to opposite sides of the atom

interactions.label: py contribution
interactions.teaches: The py contribution supplies the receding/front directional component needed for a three-dimensional tetrahedron rather than a flat arrangement

interactions.label: pz contribution
interactions.teaches: The pz contribution lifts one hybrid upward and sends others downward, producing the vertical spread of the tetrahedral set

demo_steps.title: Start with separate atomic orbitals
demo_steps.narration: The original valence orbitals are distinct: one spherical s orbital and three mutually perpendicular p orbitals. Their labels and colors emphasize that these are separate inputs before hybridization.

demo_steps.title: Mix them into four sp3 hybrids
demo_steps.narration: Hybridization combines the same four ingredients in different sign combinations. The result is four equivalent orange orbitals, each with a large lobe and a small opposite back-lobe.

demo_steps.title: Place the hybrids together
demo_steps.narration: When all four equivalent sp3 orbitals are drawn around the same atom, their large lobes point toward the corners of a tetrahedron. Orbit the view to see the full three-dimensional arrangement.

demo_steps.title: Isolate the pz role
demo_steps.narration: With only pz enabled, the vertical contribution is visible but the full tetrahedral set is lost. Turning the s, px, py, and pz contributions back on restores the equivalent sp3 hybrids.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use an axonometric chemistry-orbital style matching the source: x-axis points screen-right, z-axis screen-up, y-axis diagonally up-right/receding. Atomic-orbital view uses a 2×2 grid: s at upper left, px at upper right, py at lower left, pz at lower right. Suggested centers are (-2.2, 1.25, 0), (2.2, 1.25, 0), (-2.2, -1.25, 0), and (2.2, -1.25, 0). Each local axis triad spans about 1.25 world units from origin to arrowhead. The s orbital is a translucent blue sphere of radius about 0.42. Each p orbital is two tapered lobes of length about 0.95 and maximum radius about 0.34, meeting at the origin and aligned exactly along its named axis; use blue #4f83c4 for the positive phase and red/pink #ef6b73 for the opposite phase, with glossy translucent material. Individual sp3-hybrid view also uses a 2×2 grid, matching the right half of the source: one hybrid points mostly +z, one mostly +x, one projects down-left/back, and one projects downward/front. Each hybrid has a large orange lobe length about 1.05 and radius about 0.38, plus a small opposite back-lobe length about 0.28 and radius about 0.12. Final tetrahedral view draws all four hybrids at one origin, scaled slightly larger: large lobe length about 1.15, small back-lobe length about 0.25. Use orange/yellow #f6a21a with bright yellow highlights #ffd36b and about 0.8 opacity. The four canonical sp3 hybrids may be generated from normalized combinations h1=(s+px+py+pz)/2, h2=(s+px-py-pz)/2, h3=(s-px+py-pz)/2, h4=(s-px-py+pz)/2, then rotate the tetrahedron so one large lobe projects vertical upward like the source, one projects to the right along x, one projects down, and one projects down-left/back. The angle between any pair of large-lobe direction vectors is approximately 109.5 degrees. The contribution toggles should set the corresponding coefficient to zero before recomputing or visually decomposing the hybrid lobes; when all four are enabled, the four final hybrids must be equal size. Dominant colors: black axes and labels #000000, grey arrows/text #8a8a8a, blue s/p positive phase #4f83c4, red p phase #ef6b73, orange hybrid lobes #f6a21a with yellow center highlight.
interactionPlan.notes: Render orbitals as smooth parametric meshes or metaball-like implicit surfaces with transparent glossy materials and soft highlights. For p orbitals, create two teardrop meshes along the orbital axis rather than simple ellipsoids, so the lobes taper to the origin as in the source. For sp3 hybrids, use an angular orbital surface r proportional to max(c_s + c_x*n_x + c_y*n_y + c_z*n_z, 0)^2 for the large lobe and a smaller opposite signed lobe; rescale for readability so the figure matches the textbook proportions. Use CSS2D or signed-distance text for italic axis/orbital labels. The viewStage toggle should replace the displayed panel rather than showing all panels at once; animate the transition lightly with the grey Hybridization arrow or the downward arrow appearing between stages if desired.

discrepancies: Several sp3 hybrid lobes, especially the individual +x hybrid and parts of the final tetrahedral cluster, appear too short and round rather than elongated teardrop-shaped as in the source.
